subsystems.name: Rotor
subsystems.role: an inner loop of cable circling the planet faster than orbital speed, so it is in tension and pulls outward.

subsystems.name: Sheath
subsystems.role: a stationary ring above the rotor that carries the cities, solar arrays and launch track; the rotor presses up on it magnetically.

subsystems.name: Levitation and drive
subsystems.role: holds rotor and sheath apart without contact and spins the rotor up.

subsystems.name: Anchors and tethers
subsystems.role: optional cables hanging down to fixed ground points, which remove the need for the ring to be perfectly balanced.

subsystems.name: Launch track
subsystems.role: an electromagnetic accelerator running along the ring that flings payloads to orbital or escape velocity.

subsystems.name: Power and control
subsystems.role: supplies energy to keep the rotor spinning and steers it actively.

buildSteps.title: Make the cable
buildSteps.detail: Produce cable with a strength-to-weight ratio far beyond steel or carbon fibre — the single hardest requirement.

buildSteps.title: Launch the pieces
buildSteps.detail: Lift many payloads of cable and machinery into low Earth orbit, which needs launch costs far below today's.

buildSteps.title: Assemble in orbit
buildSteps.detail: Robots and crews join segments into a complete loop around the planet and start it moving electromagnetically.

buildSteps.title: Spin the rotor up
buildSteps.detail: Linear motors accelerate the loop past orbital velocity until its outward force can bear the weight of a stationary ring.

buildSteps.title: Add the sheath
buildSteps.detail: A second, non-moving ring is built around the rotor and levitated on magnetic fields.

buildSteps.title: Anchor to the ground
buildSteps.detail: If desired, cables are lowered and fixed to ground stations so the ring is no longer free-floating.

buildSteps.title: Build on the platform
buildSteps.detail: Habitats, farms, solar arrays and industry are assembled on the stationary ring.

buildSteps.title: Start launching
buildSteps.detail: Payloads are accelerated along the ring and released, making space access routine.

prerequisites.why: the rotor cable must hold enormous tension, and no material made today comes close to the required specific strength.

prerequisites.tech: Low-cost, high-cadence space launch and in-space assembly
prerequisites.why: many thousands of tonnes must be lifted and joined in orbit at a fraction of current cost.

prerequisites.tech: Large-scale magnetic levitation and linear motors
prerequisites.why: the rotor must be held without contact and driven continuously for years.
the ring needs continuous energy to make up losses and to launch payloads.

prerequisites.tech: Active control of a planet-scale structure
prerequisites.why: the ring must stay stable against wobbles, tidal forces and impacts for decades.

pathway.milestone: design studies of active-support structures, first proposed in the early 1980s in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society
pathway.unlocks: a shared engineering model with defined forces and materials.

pathway.milestone: small-scale rotor and levitation experiments in orbit
pathway.unlocks: data on cable strength, control and losses outside the laboratory.

pathway.milestone: a ring around an airless body such as the Moon, with no atmosphere to fight
pathway.unlocks: a first working orbital ring used for surface transport and launch.

pathway.milestone: an Earth-orbiting ring used mainly as a launcher
pathway.unlocks: very cheap access to space for power, industry and settlement.

pathway.milestone: large habitats and industry built on the stationary ring
pathway.unlocks: the 'sustainable city' idea this tile describes, if materials and launch costs are ever solved.
